opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot. If you look at where node-based workflows came from, a big part of their existence was compensating for what individual models couldn't do. You'd have one node to generate a base image, another to upscale it, another to inpaint a face that came out wrong, a ControlNet node to enforce pose, a separate model for background removal, and so on. The graph was essentially scaffolding around the limitations of each component.

As models get more capable, and you can increasingly say "give me this character, in this pose, with this lighting, and keep the identity consistent with this reference" and get something usable in one shot, a lot of that scaffolding collapses. I think a good chunk of the very intricate, hundred-node graphs people built just to get around artifacts will go away, and I'd consider that a good thing. Nobody really wanted to wire up twelve nodes to fix hands.

But I don't think node-based workflows disappear. I think their purpose shifts. Instead of being about patching model weaknesses, they become more about expressing intent and structure, especially for things that are inherently multi-step or need repeatability. If you're a studio producing hundreds of product shots that all need the same brand look, or you're building a pipeline where one generation feeds a video model which feeds an edit step, you still want something explicit, inspectable, and reproducible. A graph is a really nice representation for that. It's essentially a program that a non-programmer can read.

The other thing I'd expect is that the granularity of the nodes changes. Rather than low-level operations like "apply this LoRA at this strength" or "run this sampler for thirty steps," you'll see higher-level nodes that are more semantic: "make variations," "relight," "keep this identity," "match this style." And some of those nodes may themselves be powered by a single large model that's just being prompted differently. So the graph gets shallower and more about creative decisions than technical plumbing.

And I think there's an interesting interplay with language interfaces too. A lot of people will just talk to the model and iterate conversationally, and that's great for exploration. But once you find something you like and want to do it again, or hand it off to a teammate, you want to crystallize that into something more structured. I can easily imagine systems where your conversational session gets compiled into a workflow graph that you can then tweak and rerun. So it becomes less of an either-or between chat and nodes and more of a spectrum, from loose exploration to precise, controllable production.

So my short answer is: the nodes get bigger and smarter, the graphs get simpler, and the reason to use them moves from "the model can't do this" to "I need control, consistency, and reuse." Those needs aren't going away just because the models get better.

r001.rationale: The response says node-based workflows will not disappear as models improve, because users still need control, consistency, and reuse.

r002.rationale: It discusses exploration and iteration, but does not say that people tire of familiar results or that this drives creative boundary-pushing.

r003.rationale: It describes more capable models handling complex image requests in one shot and enabling higher-level creative workflows such as relighting, style matching, and identity control.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because on the surface it looks like these two things are in tension. You have ComfyUI-style graphs on one side, where people are wiring up dozens of nodes to get a result, and on the other side you have models like Nano Banana or the newer multimodal editors where you just type "put this person in that scene with this lighting" and it does it. So the natural assumption is that the graph is scaffolding, and as the model gets better the scaffolding comes down.

I actually don't think that's quite right. I think what happens is the graph moves up a level of abstraction. If you look at what people were doing with nodes two years ago, a lot of it was compensating for model weaknesses. You'd have a ControlNet for pose, a separate inpainting pass for hands, a face restoration step, an upscaler, and so on. Each node existed because the base model couldn't do that thing reliably. As the model absorbs those capabilities, those nodes genuinely do disappear, and that's a good thing. Nobody wants to be a plumber.

But the reason people reach for a graph in the first place isn't just patching weaknesses. It's control and repeatability. If you're a professional, you don't want one image, you want a process you can run on a hundred assets with the same look, and you want to be able to go back and change one decision without redoing everything. That's a workflow problem, not a model-capability problem, and better one-shot models don't solve it. If anything they make it more acute, because now the model is doing more inside a single black box and you have less visibility into the intermediate state.

So my guess is the nodes become less about "denoise step, VAE decode, upscale" and more about semantic operations. A node that's "establish the character," a node that's "apply this lighting setup," a node that's "generate variations under these constraints," where each of those is itself a pretty powerful model call. The graph becomes a way to structure intent and manage state across a project rather than a way to assemble a pipeline out of parts.

The other thing I'd say is that the research side and the tooling side are kind of chasing each other. A lot of the things that got built as nodes, like reference-based editing or multi-image composition, became training targets, and then they got folded into the model. And I expect that to keep happening. So the graph is also a kind of early warning system for what the next generation of models should do natively. The things people keep rebuilding by hand are the things we should be training.

And honestly, I think the convergence point is something more conversational on top with something more structured underneath. For a casual user, the chat interface wins, no question. But for someone doing real production work, there's going to be a layer where you can see and edit the actual structure of what the system did, and that will look a lot like a node graph, even if nobody calls it that.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that node graphs will remain useful for production work, evolving from technical pipelines into structures for managing intent and state as models improve.

r002.rationale: It does not mention people tiring of familiar results or connect that tendency to creative boundary-pushing.

r003.rationale: It describes more capable model calls and professional workflows, but does not clearly argue that improved tools expand the possibilities for advanced creative work.

astra-6.text:
I think the workflows will become simpler, but I don’t think the need for control goes away. A lot of nodes today exist because you have to break a task into pieces that the model can handle. As models get better at doing those things together, you can collapse parts of that graph into a single step.

But there’s a difference between getting a good image in one shot and getting exactly the image you want. If you’re iterating on something, you may want to change the lighting while keeping the composition, or change one object while preserving everything else. You still need a way to express those constraints and make the process repeatable.

So I’d expect the nodes to become higher-level. You spend less time wiring together the mechanics of generation and more time specifying the creative decisions you want to control. For some people, that will just be a conversation with the model. For others, an explicit workflow will still be useful because it lets them see, reuse, and adjust those decisions.

r001.rationale: It says nodes will become higher-level and explicit workflows will remain useful for people who want to see, reuse, and adjust creative decisions.

r002.rationale: It does not mention people tiring of familiar results or that this drives them to push creative boundaries.

r003.rationale: It describes models simplifying workflows and preserving control, but does not say more capable tools expand possibilities for advanced creative work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the workflows will become simpler as the models become more capable. A lot of what you’re doing in a node graph today is explicitly breaking a task into steps and wiring those steps together. If a model can handle several of those steps in one shot, you don’t necessarily need to expose all that complexity to the user.

But I don’t think that means node-based workflows disappear. They’re useful when you want control over an intermediate result, or when you want to repeat a process reliably. You might want to say, “Keep this part fixed, change this other part, and run these three variations.” Having an explicit workflow can still be valuable there.

So I’d expect the nodes to operate at a higher level. Instead of managing every little operation, you’re composing larger capabilities, with the ability to go deeper when you need to. The interesting question is how much control you can preserve while making the common case much easier.

r001.rationale: It says node-based workflows will not disappear and remain useful for control and repeatable processes as models take on more steps.

r002.rationale: It does not mention people tiring of familiar results or that this drives continued creative boundary-pushing.

r003.rationale: It describes composing larger capabilities and retaining control, but does not clearly argue that more capable tools expand possibilities for advanced creative work.
